deep_reading.title: Coarse-to-Fine Long-term Interest Modeling for Generative Recommendation
deep_reading.content:
Generative recommendation encodes each item as a few levels of semantic IDs (SIDs) and uses a Transformer to generate the next item one code at a time. Attention cost grows quadratically with sequence length, so these models usually take only the most recent few dozen behaviors. In the paper's two datasets, the average user history length is 987 (TAOBAO-MM) and 884 (KuaiRec), yet the model input keeps only the last 50. The authors also observe a pattern: in plain generative retrieval, after the first-level code is generated, the true item's rank in the beam gets worse rather than better, with the average rank dropping by 1.25 at the second level. GLASS ==uses the long-term history differently for each SID level==: before generating the first-level code, it compresses the whole long-term history into one interest token fed to the encoder; after the first-level code is generated, it uses that code as a retrieval key to pull items of the same broad category from the long-term history, which help generate the last two codes. On TAOBAO-MM, R@1 is 21.57% higher than the strongest baseline, DualGR; in a two-week A/B test on a short-video platform, app usage time per user rose 0.052% and recall rose 3 percentage points in absolute terms.

## 1. The problem: getting long histories into generative retrieval

The ranking stage has a mature recipe for long sequences, SIM's two-stage design: a GSU (General Search Unit) first uses the target item to retrieve a relevant sub-sequence from the long history, then an ESU (Exact Search Unit) runs fine-grained target attention over it. The retrieval stage has no target item, so the GSU has nothing to search with. OneRec and OneSearch use a Q-Former to compress long-term behavior into fixed-length vectors, which stops at the granularity of interest clusters. DualGR already uses SIDs as retrieval keys in generative retrieval, but it treats codes at every level the same way.

The authors start from the structure of SIDs themselves. The first-level code decides which broad category an item belongs to, and the last two codes locate the specific item inside that category. When the first-level code is generated there is no path yet, so the model needs the user's overall preference across categories; when the last two codes are generated the category is fixed, so the model needs what the user actually engaged with inside that category. ==The two levels need long-term information at different granularity, so it is injected in two places==.

## 2. Overall structure

![The three parts of GLASS. On the left, (a) is the encoder-decoder backbone: the short-term sequence goes through a lookup table and self-attention into the encoder, and the SID-Tier at the bottom right outputs one token appended after the short-term sequence; each decoder layer has two cross-attention paths, one over the encoder output and one over the long-term items returned by Semantic Search, and the Gate in the middle merges them with weights g and 1−g. Top right, (b) is SID-Tier: similarity is computed between each first-level code and every item in the long-term history, counted into a histogram by similarity bin, normalized, and passed through an MLP. Bottom right, (c) is semantic search: the generated first-level code <a_5> hard-matches items in the long-term history whose first-level code is the same (Item1, Item3), and neighboring codes <a_2> and <a_8> are added when there are too few.](figs/recsys26-glass/fig1.jpg)

The backbone is a TIGER-style encoder-decoder. Each item's multimodal vector is quantized by RQ-VAE into three levels of codes; on the public datasets the codebook sizes are [64,128,128], the embedding dimension is 96, and the encoder and decoder each have 4 layers. The user history is sorted by time and split in two: the most recent 50 behaviors are the short-term sequence, and everything earlier is the long-term sequence.

## 3. First-level code: SID-Tier compresses the long-term history into one token

This step addresses the fact that the first-level code is generated with no clue at all. Running attention directly over the long-term history is too expensive, so the authors exploit the small size of the first-level codebook: there are only tens to a little over a hundred first-level codes, so cross features between the user history and every code can all be computed.

Each first-level code $k$ first gets a prototype vector $\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_k$, the mean of the vectors of all items whose first-level code is $k$. The cosine-similarity range $[-1,1]$ is then split evenly into $N$ bins, and for each first-level code the model counts how many long-term history items fall into each bin:

$$\mathbf{t}_k[j]=\sum_{v\in H^{id}_{long}}\mathbb{I}\big(\text{bin}(\text{Cos}(\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_k,\mathbf{h}_v))=j\big)$$

$\mathbf{h}_v$ is the multimodal vector of history item $v$, $\text{bin}(\cdot)$ maps a similarity to its bin, and $\mathbb{I}$ is the indicator function. Intuitively, $\mathbf{t}_k$ describes how many items in the user's history are very similar to category $k$, how many are somewhat similar, and how many are not. The histograms of all first-level codes are concatenated into a vector of length $K_0\cdot N$, compressed by an MLP (hidden size 256) into one $d$-dimensional vector $\mathbf{e}_{tier}$, and appended after the short-term sequence embedding before entering the encoder.

This token depends only on the user history and the codebook, not on the item being generated, so it can be precomputed offline. It is really the familiar "user's historical preference statistics per category" feature from ranking models, computed over first-level SID codes instead.

## 4. The last two codes: retrieve from the long-term history with the generated first-level code

After the first-level code $\hat{c}_0$ is generated, the model takes every item in the long-term history with the same first-level code:

$$H_{ret}=\{c(v_i)\mid v_i\in H^{id}_{long},\ c_0(v_i)=\hat{c}_0(v_{n+1})\}$$

This is SIM's hard search with the key changed from "the target item's category" to "the first-level code just generated". Each decoder layer runs self-attention and then two cross-attention paths in parallel: one with the encoder output as key/value, giving $\mathbf{Z}_{short}$; one with the retrieved item embeddings as key/value, giving $\mathbf{Z}_{ret}$. A gate merges the two:

$$\mathbf{g}=\sigma([\mathbf{Z}_{short};\mathbf{Z}_{ret}]\mathbf{W}_g),\qquad \mathbf{Z}_{context}=(\mathbf{1}-\mathbf{g})\odot\mathbf{Z}_{short}+\mathbf{g}\odot\mathbf{Z}_{ret}$$

$\mathbf{W}_g$ is a $2d\times d$ projection and $\sigma$ is the sigmoid. A large $\mathbf{g}$ tilts the result toward the retrieved long-term items; a small $\mathbf{g}$ tilts it toward the short-term sequence. The training objective is the standard autoregressive cross-entropy over the three codes.

## 5. What if too few items come back

Hard search has an obvious problem. In the paper's example, with a history of 1000 and a first-level codebook of 128, each first-level code retrieves only about 7.8 items on average: too little information, with a high share of noise. The authors offer two fixes:

- **Semantic neighbor augmentation**: precompute cosine similarities between first-level codes and record each code's top-k nearest neighbors. When fewer items than a threshold $\tau$ come back, the history items under the neighbor codes are merged in as well.
- **Shrinking the first-level codebook**: make the first-level codebook smaller during training so that each first-level code covers more items. The first level is responsible for volume, the last two for precision.

## 6. Experiments

**Main results**. The goal is to show that GLASS beats both ID-based sequential models and SID-based generative models. Both datasets keep only positive feedback: TAOBAO-MM keeps clicks, uniformly samples 10,000 items and keeps those that appear at least 5 times in the training set; KuaiRec keeps samples whose play time exceeds the video length. The table below takes, from the paper's Table 2, the strongest ID model HSTU and two SID baselines: TIGER is standard generative retrieval, and DualGR uses separate long- and short-term branches with routing.

| Dataset | Model | R@1 | R@5 | R@10 | N@10 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| TAOBAO-MM | HSTU | 0.0274 | 0.0512 | 0.0784 | 0.0495 |
| TAOBAO-MM | TIGER | 0.0280 | 0.0756 | 0.1076 | 0.0627 |
| TAOBAO-MM | DualGR | 0.0306 | 0.0781 | 0.1126 | 0.0653 |
| TAOBAO-MM | GLASS | 0.0372 | 0.0934 | 0.1284 | 0.0782 |
| KuaiRec | HSTU | 0.0334 | 0.0845 | 0.1183 | 0.0704 |
| KuaiRec | TIGER | 0.0406 | 0.0859 | 0.1202 | 0.0751 |
| KuaiRec | DualGR | 0.0445 | 0.0932 | 0.1292 | 0.0821 |
| KuaiRec | GLASS | 0.0467 | 0.0971 | 0.1345 | 0.0855 |

On KuaiRec the gain is only 3.81%–4.94%. The authors attribute this to KuaiRec's multimodal vectors coming from a simple text encoding, which gives poorer SIDs, whereas TAOBAO-MM uses multimodal features trained with contrastive learning.

**Which level each module helps**. This ablation shows that SID-Tier mainly helps the first-level code and semantic search mainly helps the second. The authors track two quantities: $acc_i$, the training accuracy of the level-$i$ code under teacher forcing, and $P_i$, the probability that the level-$i$ code is also correct under top-1 beam search given all earlier levels are correct. Adding SID-Tier raises $acc_1$ from 0.2410 to 0.2485, $P_1$ from 0.1470 to 0.1587, and Recall@5 from 0.0702 to 0.0842. Adding semantic search on top mainly lifts $acc_2$ and $P_2$.

![Ablation results. The top panel shows Recall and NDCG for four configurations; the bottom panel shows training accuracy acc and inference precision P for the level-1 and level-2 codes. Dark blue removes both modules, light blue adds only SID-Tier, red adds only semantic search, and orange is full GLASS. In the bottom panel, light blue mainly lifts acc1 and P1 over dark blue, while red mainly lifts acc2 and P2: the two modules act on different levels.](figs/recsys26-glass/fig2.jpg)

**Why the rank drops**. The authors define Conditional Rank Progression (CRP): over samples whose first $d-1$ codes all stayed in the beam, the average rank of the correct level-$d$ code among the top-K candidates; closer to 1 is better. With beam size 20, the plain generative model's rank worsens by 1.25 on average at the second level, and only by 0.98 with semantic search; at the third level the worsening falls from 0.19 to 0.13. The cause is that when a plain model generates the last two codes, its conditioning context is still the original one, with no new information to widen the probability gap between the right answer and the distractors.

**Does the gate matter**. A fixed weight of 0.5 helps when the first-level codebook is small but hurts once the codebook gets finer, because retrieved-sequence length varies a lot, and when it is too short the noise flows straight into beam search's cumulative probabilities. The learned gate value rises overall with retrieval length: ==the more items are retrieved, the more weight the model puts on the long-term branch==.

![Average gate value at inference versus retrieved sequence length; the blue line is the setup with all three codebooks of size 128, the red line the setup with a first-level codebook of 64 and 128 for the last two. Both lines rise from left to right, and the gate value is highest at retrieval length 30.](figs/recsys26-glass/fig4.jpg)

**Sparsity fixes**. Shrinking the first-level codebook gave the best Recall@10. Semantic neighbor augmentation helps only without codebook shrinking; adding neighbors on top of a shrunken codebook lowers the metrics slightly, which the authors attribute to neighbor items blurring the boundaries between different interests.

**Online**. A two-week A/B test on a short-video platform, with 3% of users (about 12 million) in each of the treatment and control groups. At 95% confidence, total app usage time rose 0.056%, app usage time per user rose 0.052%, and recall rose 3 percentage points in absolute terms.

## 7. Limitations and what to try

The paper has no separate limitations discussion; two facts are worth keeping in mind. The public datasets are small: KuaiRec has only 3790 users and TAOBAO-MM's items are sampled down to 10,000, far from industrial codebook scale. Results are sensitive to SID quality: on TAOBAO-MM each metric improves 14.03%–29.91% over the strongest baseline, on KuaiRec only 3.81%–4.94%.

If you work on generative retrieval and have long behavior sequences, two things are worth trying directly:

- Append the "user's historical preference histogram over first-level codes" as an extra token to the encoder input; it can be computed offline and adds almost no online cost.
- Before doing hard search with the generated first-level code, measure how many items each first-level code retrieves from user histories on average; if too few, try shrinking the first-level codebook first and neighbor augmentation second.

papers.title: GenPage: Towards End-to-End Generative Homepage Construction at Netflix
papers.authors: Lequn Wang, Jiangwei Pan, Linas Baltrunas
papers.summary: The Netflix homepage consists of rows, each with a theme and a set of titles, and it used to be assembled by several stages such as a row model and an entity model. GenPage encodes the user's viewing history, device, time of day and so on as tokens forming a prompt, and a ~200M-parameter decoder-only Transformer generates row and title tokens one by one, left to right and top to bottom. ==Every row and every title is a single token, so business rules can be written directly as a candidate mask at each step==. In an online A/B test the core metric used for launch decisions rose 0.24% and end-to-end latency fell 20%; offline, enriching the prompt reduced the loss more than scaling the model from 120M to 900M parameters.
papers.abstract: GenPage replaces Netflix's multi-stage homepage recommender with a transformer that autoregressively generates an entire structured multi-row homepage. It is pretrained on positively engaged production pages and post-trained using weighted binary classification or reinforcement learning, with mechanisms for cold start, freshness, business rules, and serving efficiency. Online A/B tests report a 0.24% engagement lift and 20% lower end-to-end latency.

papers.abstract: Generative recommendation is a coarse-to-fine process in which Semantic ID prefixes determine broad categories and suffixes identify items. GLASS injects distinct long-term user signals into these stages through SID-Tier for prefix generation and semantic hard search with gated fusion for suffix generation. Experiments on TAOBAO-MM and KuaiRec outperform prior baselines, and a two-week online A/B test on a short-video platform reports significant recommendation-quality gains.

In the bottom panel, light blue mainly lifts acc1 and P1 over dark blue, while red mainly lifts acc2 and P2: the two modules act on different levels.](figs/recsys26-glass/fig2.jpg)

**Why the rank drops**. The authors define Conditional Rank Progression (CRP): over samples whose first $d-1$ codes all stayed in the beam, the average rank of the correct level-$d$ code among the top-K candidates; closer to 1 is better. With beam size 20, the plain generative model's rank worsens by 1.25 on average at the second level, and only by 0.98 with semantic search; at the third level the worsening falls from 0.19 to 0.13. The cause is that when a plain model generates the last two codes, its conditioning context is still the original one, with no new information to widen the probability gap between the right answer and the distractors.

**Does the gate matter**. A fixed weight of 0.5 helps when the first-level codebook is small but hurts once the codebook gets finer, because retrieved-sequence length varies a lot, and when it is too short the noise flows straight into beam search's cumulative probabilities. The learned gate value rises overall with retrieval length: ==the more items are retrieved, the more weight the model puts on the long-term branch==.

Both lines rise from left to right, and the gate value is highest at retrieval length 30.](figs/recsys26-glass/fig4.jpg)

**Sparsity fixes**. Shrinking the first-level codebook gave the best Recall@10. Semantic neighbor augmentation helps only without codebook shrinking; adding neighbors on top of a shrunken codebook lowers the metrics slightly, which the authors attribute to neighbor items blurring the boundaries between different interests.

**Online**. A two-week A/B test on a short-video platform, with 3% of users (about 12 million) in each of the treatment and control groups. At 95% confidence, total app usage time rose 0.056%, app usage time per user rose 0.052%, and recall rose 3 percentage points in absolute terms.

## 7. Limitations and what to try

The paper has no separate limitations discussion; two facts are worth keeping in mind. The public datasets are small: KuaiRec has only 3790 users and TAOBAO-MM's items are sampled down to 10,000, far from industrial codebook scale. Results are sensitive to SID quality: on TAOBAO-MM each metric improves 14.03%–29.91% over the strongest baseline, on KuaiRec only 3.81%–4.94%.

If you work on generative retrieval and have long behavior sequences, two things are worth trying directly:

- Append the "user's historical preference histogram over first-level codes" as an extra token to the encoder input; it can be computed offline and adds almost no online cost.
- Before doing hard search with the generated first-level code, measure how many items each first-level code retrieves from user histories on average; if too few, try shrinking the first-level codebook first and neighbor augmentation second.

Generative recommendation encodes each item as a few levels of semantic IDs (SIDs) and uses a Transformer to generate the next item one code at a time. The authors also observe a pattern: in plain generative retrieval, after the first-level code is generated, the true item's rank in the beam gets worse rather than better, with the average rank dropping by 1.25 at the second level. GLASS uses the long-term history differently for each SID level: before generating the first-level code, it compresses the whole long-term history into one interest token fed to the encoder; after the first-level code is generated, it uses that code as a retrieval key to pull items of the same broad category from the long-term history, which help generate the last two codes. On TAOBAO-MM, R@1 is 21.57% higher than the strongest baseline, DualGR; in a two-week A/B test on a short-video platform, app usage time per user rose 0.052% and recall rose 3 percentage points in absolute terms.

1. The problem: getting long histories into generative retrieval

The ranking stage has a mature recipe for long sequences, SIM's two-stage design: a GSU (General Search Unit) first uses the target item to retrieve a relevant sub-sequence from the long history, then an ESU (Exact Search Unit) runs fine-grained target attention over it. The retrieval stage has no target item, so the GSU has nothing to search with. OneRec and OneSearch use a Q-Former to compress long-term behavior into fixed-length vectors, which stops at the granularity of interest clusters. DualGR already uses SIDs as retrieval keys in generative retrieval, but it treats codes at every level the same way.

The authors start from the structure of SIDs themselves. The first-level code decides which broad category an item belongs to, and the last two codes locate the specific item inside that category. When the first-level code is generated there is no path yet, so the model needs the user's overall preference across categories; when the last two codes are generated the category is fixed, so the model needs what the user actually engaged with inside that category. The two levels need long-term information at different granularity, so it is injected in two places.

2. Overall structure

The backbone is a TIGER-style encoder-decoder. Each item's multimodal vector is quantized by RQ-VAE into three levels of codes; on the public datasets the codebook sizes are [64,128,128], the embedding dimension is 96, and the encoder and decoder each have 4 layers. The user history is sorted by time and split in two: the most recent 50 behaviors are the short-term sequence, and everything earlier is the long-term sequence.

3. First-level code: SID-Tier compresses the long-term history into one token

This step addresses the fact that the first-level code is generated with no clue at all. Running attention directly over the long-term history is too expensive, so the authors exploit the small size of the first-level codebook: there are only tens to a little over a hundred first-level codes, so cross features between the user history and every code can all be computed.

Each first-level code k first gets a prototype vector h~k​, the mean of the vectors of all items whose first-level code is k. The cosine-similarity range $[-1,1]$ is then split evenly into N bins, and for each first-level code the model counts how many long-term history items fall into each bin:
tk​[j]=v∈Hlongid​∑​I(bin(Cos(h~k​,hv​))=j)
hv​ is the multimodal vector of history item v, bin(⋅) maps a similarity to its bin, and I is the indicator function. Intuitively, tk​ describes how many items in the user's history are very similar to category k, how many are somewhat similar, and how many are not. The histograms of all first-level codes are concatenated into a vector of length K0​⋅N, compressed by an MLP (hidden size 256) into one d-dimensional vector etier​, and appended after the short-term sequence embedding before entering the encoder.

This token depends only on the user history and the codebook, not on the item being generated, so it can be precomputed offline. It is really the familiar "user's historical preference statistics per category" feature from ranking models, computed over first-level SID codes instead.

4. The last two codes: retrieve from the long-term history with the generated first-level code

After the first-level code c^0​ is generated, the model takes every item in the long-term history with the same first-level code:
Hret​={c(vi​)∣vi​∈Hlongid​, c0​(vi​)=c^0​(vn+1​)}
This is SIM's hard search with the key changed from "the target item's category" to "the first-level code just generated". Each decoder layer runs self-attention and then two cross-attention paths in parallel: one with the encoder output as key/value, giving Zshort​; one with the retrieved item embeddings as key/value, giving Zret​. A gate merges the two:
g=σ([Zshort​;Zret​]Wg​),Zcontext​=(1−g)⊙Zshort​+g⊙Zret​
Wg​ is a 2d×d projection and σ is the sigmoid. A large g tilts the result toward the retrieved long-term items; a small g tilts it toward the short-term sequence. The training objective is the standard autoregressive cross-entropy over the three codes.

5. What if too few items come back

Hard search has an obvious problem. In the paper's example, with a history of 1000 and a first-level codebook of 128, each first-level code retrieves only about 7.8 items on average: too little information, with a high share of noise. The authors offer two fixes:

  • Semantic neighbor augmentation: precompute cosine similarities between first-level codes and record each code's top-k nearest neighbors. When fewer items than a threshold τ come back, the history items under the neighbor codes are merged in as well.
  • Shrinking the first-level codebook: make the first-level codebook smaller during training so that each first-level code covers more items. The first level is responsible for volume, the last two for precision.

papers.title: CSG4Rec: Collaborative-Similarity Guided Semantic IDs Tokenization for Generative Sequential Recommendation
papers.authors: Wei Liu, Bo Yang, Qianyang Zhu, Ruijie Xiao, Sirui Huang, Qing Li
papers.summary: The semantic IDs used in generative sequential recommendation are usually produced by quantizing item text embeddings layer by layer, so items with similar text get similar codes; collaborative information such as "often bought by the same users" never enters the codes. CSG4Rec adds a contrastive loss when training the tokenizer: the quantized vectors of two items with similar collaborative behavior are pulled together and those of dissimilar items are pushed apart, ==so that items with similar codes are similar in both text and user behavior==. It also aggregates the embeddings of each user's historically interacted items and quantizes them into a user semantic ID, which is fed into the generative model together with the item semantic IDs. The authors report gains over existing baselines on three benchmark datasets.
papers.abstract: The paper proposes collaborative-similarity guided semantic-ID tokenization that fuses semantic and collaborative information in one space. It also constructs user semantic IDs to capture preference characteristics and builds CSG4Rec for generative sequential recommendation. The method is designed to address the mismatch between content-derived identifiers and collaborative behavior signals.

papers.title: Topology-Aware Tokenization for Generative Recommendation
papers.summary: Generative recommenders first use RQ-VAE to quantize each item's semantic embedding layer by layer into a code sequence (a semantic ID), but quantization scrambles neighbor relations between items: of an item's top-20 neighbors in the original embedding space, only 63% are still in the top 20 after layer-1 codes, and only 27% by layer 3. TopoTok adds a KL loss at each layer when training the tokenizer so that neighbor rankings after quantization match those of the original embeddings: layer 1 aligns distances between code groups (items sharing the same layer-1 code), layer 2 aligns distances among items in the same layer-1 group, and layer 3 aligns distances among all items. ==Constraints go from coarse to fine by layer because early RQ-VAE layers only separate broad categories and later layers separate individual items==. On TIGER (a generative recommender that uses T5 to generate semantic IDs token by token), Recall@5 on Amazon Scientific rises from 0.0275 to 0.0302; the losses are computed only in training and add no inference cost.
papers.abstract: Generative recommendation reframes sequential recommendation as autoregressive generation over discrete item identifiers. This work identifies topology distortion in semantic-ID tokenization: adjacency relationships in continuous item-embedding space can be disrupted after quantization. It develops topology-aware tokenization to preserve local item structure for autoregressive prediction and evaluates the approach in generative recommendation settings.

papers.title: Evaluating LLM-based conversational recommenders with semantic and genre-aware metrics
papers.authors: Darshna Parmar, Dhruv Shah, Pramit Mazumdar, Saurav Mallik
papers.summary: In conversational recommendation, Recall@K and BLEU count an LLM's movie suggestion as wrong whenever it is not the exact labeled answer, even if both are action comedies. The authors find that the labeled answer appears in the top 10 recommendations only 39% of the time, while another 53% of recommendations share at least a genre with the answer. They build one unified pipeline: a prompt extracts titles, genres and actors from the user's words, these are used to filter candidate movies from a knowledge graph, and an LLM generates the reply; six instruction-tuned models are compared on two movie dialogue datasets, ReDial and INSPIRED. Two new metrics, GHR@10 and SoftGHR@10, score whether the top 10 recommendations overlap the answer in genre, with SoftGHR also crediting partial overlap. The authors conclude that ==recommendation quality and fabrication depend on the knowledge graph and dialogue context, not on model size==.
papers.abstract: Conversational recommender systems powered by large language models generate fluent dialogue but remain difficult to evaluate with lexical metrics. This study benchmarks systems on ReDial and INSPIRED using a pipeline that combines natural-language understanding, dialogue management, knowledge-graph reasoning and LLM generation. It introduces genre-aware measures for preference alignment and analyzes how model size, knowledge grounding and context affect quality and hallucination.

papers.title: Integrating implicit desire fusion for proactive conversational recommendation systems with LLMs
papers.authors: Sitong Yan, Shengli Song, Chengen Lai, Jingyang Li, Guangneng Hu
papers.summary: In conversational recommendation, users often cannot say what they want, and asking about attributes turn after turn drags the dialogue out. DESIRE trains no model; it uses LLMs such as GPT-3.5-Turbo with prompts to handle each turn: it first summarizes the dialogue context, the user's historical preferences, attributes retrieved from the item database and this turn's accept or reject feedback into a needs description, then decides whether to keep asking or to recommend; when asking it picks one of five question types, when recommending it picks one of six persuasion strategies such as presenting evidence or social proof, and item attributes in the reply may only come from retrieval results. Evaluation uses an LLM-simulated user. On LastFM the success rate within 15 turns (SR@15) is 0.583, versus 0.544 for the multi-agent baseline MACRS; removing the needs-summary step drops it to 0.327, ==showing that the success rate mainly comes from summarizing multiple signals first and then deciding whether to ask or recommend==.
papers.abstract: The paper introduces DESIRE, a desire-oriented conversational recommendation framework combining implicit desire exploration with recommendation strategy planning. It targets precision, proactivity and persuasion in user-centric dialogue. Evaluation on LastFM and Yelp reports improved recommendation quality and dialogue persuasiveness in music and e-commerce scenarios.

papers.title: Unleashing the Native Recommendation Potential: LLM-Based Generative Recommendation via Structured Term Identifiers
papers.summary: When LLMs do generative recommendation, item IDs usually take one of two forms: generating titles directly, whose huge output space makes it easy to invent nonexistent items, or numeric semantic IDs from quantization, which require adding new tokens to the vocabulary plus extra alignment training. Kuaishou's GRLM instead uses 5 standardized keywords as the item ID (e.g., "Cell-Phone | iPhone 17 Pro | 120Hz | Apple AI"). When generating the keywords, the information of the items with the most similar embeddings is put into the prompt as well, ==so that similar items use the same wording and each item's differences are also written into its keywords==. Qwen3-4B is fully fine-tuned on two tasks at once: writing keywords from item information, and predicting the next item's keywords from user history. At inference, items are first matched by exact string; if none matches, keywords are compared one by one, with earlier keywords weighted more. On Amazon Sports, Recall@5 is 0.0375, 30.21% above OneRec-Think, which needs vocabulary expansion; over 98.9% of generated IDs map to real items in the catalog.
papers.abstract: The paper introduces structured Term IDs made from semantically rich standardized textual keywords as item identifiers for LLM-based generative recommendation. Textual identifiers constrain the output space while avoiding the semantic gap and vocabulary-expansion costs associated with opaque semantic IDs, enabling language models to use native vocabulary for recommendation.

papers.title: HARPO: Hierarchical Agentic Reasoning for User-Aligned Conversational Recommendation
papers.summary: Conversational recommenders are usually evaluated with Recall@K and BLEU, and the authors argue that high scores on these metrics do not mean the recommendations fit what users want. HARPO applies LoRA fine-tuning to DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B; before each reply it expands several candidate reasoning paths (beam width 3, depth 3), a value network scores each path on four dimensions—relevance, diversity, satisfaction and engagement—and the highest-scoring path generates the reply. The four reward heads are first trained on preference pairs made of one better and one worse reply, the value network then learns from the reward heads' scores, and the dimension weights change with the dialogue context. On ReDial, Recall@10 is 29.8%, versus 25.1% for the strongest baseline DCRS and 21.6% for supervised fine-tuning alone on the same backbone. ==Satisfaction and engagement are scored by the same reward model HARPO optimizes during training, so comparing methods with it favors HARPO==; the authors add a human evaluation of 200 samples per dataset.
papers.abstract: Conversational recommendation operates under incremental preference revelation and uncertainty. HARPO uses hierarchical agentic reasoning to optimize user-aligned recommendation outcomes rather than relying only on proxy metrics such as Recall@K or dialogue fluency. The work evaluates recommendation decisions and alignment in conversational settings.
